faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other. As they orbit, one star periodically passes in front of the other as seen from Earth, blocking some of its light. This causes the star's brightness to dip in a regular, predictable pattern. By measuring these dips in brightness over time - a light curve - astronomers can learn about the stars' sizes, orbits, and how they interact.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?

faqs.answer: A candidate is a star whose light curve shows eclipse-like dips and has passed our statistical tests and catalog cross-checks. A confirmed result is a candidate that has also passed our automated pixel-level check, which ensures the signal is really there and really centered on the target star, not caused by a nearby star or instrumental noise. Only confirmed candidates appear in our main results list.
faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' result on this site?

faqs.answer: It is a second opinion from a machine learning model trained on 2889 labeled examples. The model learned which candidates are most likely to pass pixel-level vetting. Its score helps you gauge confidence in a candidate, and it performs better than our default rule-based approach. However, the model does not decide which candidates get checked - all candidates passing our statistical gates and novelty cross-match go to the pixel check regardless of any ML score.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning score I see on candidate pages?

faqs.answer: Every candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check. This check examines whether the eclipse signal is truly centered on the target star or whether it comes from a nearby star, instrumental artifacts, or noise. It is fully automated - no human eye reviews it. A candidate must pass this check to be listed as confirmed on our site.
faqs.question: How are candidates checked for false alarms?

faqs.answer: We perform an odd/even eclipse-depth test: we compare the depth of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses to detect period aliases - cases where the true orbital period is actually half (or a simple multiple of) what we initially measured. If this test raises a flag, that caveat is noted on the candidate's individual page, and you should be aware of the ambiguity when considering the result.
faqs.question: What happens if a candidate's eclipse period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Yes. We provide links to the TESS light curve data and to our pixel-level check images for each confirmed candidate. You can download the data and examine it yourself using public tools, inspect the images, and form your own judgment about whether the signal is real and on-target.
faqs.question: Can I verify a confirmed candidate myself?

faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the end of this pipeline's process. We do not perform spectroscopy, radial-velocity measurements, or any follow-up observations. We do not submit candidates to other databases, coordinate follow-up studies, or track their fate in the scientific community. The site serves as a catalog of candidates that have passed our vetting for anyone - professional or amateur - who wishes to study or follow up on them independently.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed on this site?

faqs.answer: We have sampled 19421 target stars out of 872720 available in TESS, covering approximately 2.2% of the full target list. The project is ongoing, and more targets will be processed over time.
faqs.question: How much of the sky has you checked so far?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically vets candidate eclipsing binary stars found in data from NASA's TESS satellite. An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars that orbit each other and pass in front of each other as seen from Earth, causing regular dips in brightness. Our pipeline samples target stars, retrieves their light curves, applies statistical tests to spot eclipse-like patterns, cross-checks them against six known variable-star catalogs to find novel candidates, and then runs an automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal is real and on-target rather than a false alarm from nearby stars or noise. So far we have confirmed 279 candidates. Every candidate that passes our statistical gates and finds no match in existing catalogs goes through the pixel check. We also train a machine learning model as a second opinion to understand which candidates are most reliable, but the model itself does not gate which candidates get checked. The combination of automated vetting, multi-catalog cross-matching, and pixel-level confirmation gives us confidence in what we list, though individual candidates may carry open caveats noted on their pages.
